newsitem.title: GERMANY: Trichet sure of final deal on stability pact.
newsitem.headline: Trichet sure of final deal on stability pact.

text.p: Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet said on Wednesday he had "no doubt" European countries would iron out their differences and agree a stability pact to enforce fiscal discipline under monetary union.
Trichet, speaking to Germany's Die Zeit weekly, also said there was no need to alter the exchange rate between the French franc and the German mark.

He said hard bargaining over Germany's call for a tough stability pact with automatic penalties for countries which violate the Maastricht treaty's tight fiscal limits after monetary union was a matter "of definition".

"We all support, in certain cases, fines against budget sinners for the sake of the euro's stability. We just have to decide when sanctions should apply automatically and when a political judgement is needed," he told Die Zeit.
"I haven't the slightest doubt that the partner countries will eventually reach an agreement," he added. Trichet's remarks were published in German.

The European Union's monetary committee met in Brussels on Wednesday to try to finalise a compromise stability pact ahead of a summit in Dublin this Friday where leaders will review a new draft EU treaty designed to cope with future enlargement.

One stumbling block has been a demand by Germany for agreement that numbers alone should determine whether a country in recession would be permitted to exceed Maastricht's three percent budget deficit limit without incurring a penalty. Most other EU states want scope for political judgement.
Trichet rejected calls from French eurosceptics for a franc devaluation, saying that 80 percent of his country's economic problems were structural, not cyclical.
Former President Valery Giscard d'Estaing, along with some monetary policy council members of the French central bank, have said the franc was overvalued in relation to the U.S. dollar.
They have called for a devaluation to give the French economy scope to reduce chronically high unemployment and ease labour tensions.
But Trichet rejected their arguments: "The small minority of opponents to Maastricht which is attacking monetary policy is really targetting European unity," he told Die Zeit.
"We are highly competitive, we have a balance of payments surplus, our inflation is among the lowest, and all factors for a strong inflation-free recovery are in place.
"We are at least as attached to our franc as the Germans are to their mark."
Trichet is due to hold a speech in Bonn on Thursday evening, the day before the Dublin summit. The speech is entitled "Unity and Stability in Europe, a French Central Bank Perspective".
